questions.stem: A student removes all the stamens from a flower before the anthers open and then covers the flower with a bag. No seeds develop. What does this experiment demonstrate?

options.text: The flower needed water to produce seeds
The flower needed its own pollen or pollen from another flower to produce seeds, and the bag prevented pollination
Removing the stamens damaged the ovary, preventing seed formation
The petals are essential for seed production

questions.explanation: By removing the stamens (which produce pollen) and covering the flower (preventing external pollen from arriving), the student prevented pollination entirely. Without pollination, fertilisation cannot occur, and no seeds develop. This demonstrates that pollen is essential for sexual reproduction in flowering plants.

questions.stem: Insect-pollinated flowers typically have large, brightly coloured petals and produce nectar, while wind-pollinated flowers often have small, dull petals. Which explanation best accounts for these differences?

options.text: Insect-pollinated flowers need to attract insects with colour and nectar rewards; wind-pollinated flowers do not need to attract animals
Wind-pollinated flowers have small petals so the wind can blow them away more easily
Insect-pollinated flowers are newer in evolution and have not yet adapted to wind
Large petals help insect-pollinated flowers photosynthesize more efficiently

questions.explanation: Insect-pollinated flowers have evolved bright colours, scent, and nectar to attract insect pollinators, which carry pollen between flowers. Wind-pollinated flowers do not need these features because they rely on wind to carry pollen. Instead, they have adaptations like long dangling stamens and feathery stigmas to catch airborne pollen.

questions.stem: A flower has anthers that mature and release pollen before the stigma of the same flower becomes receptive. What is the advantage of this timing?

options.text: It ensures the flower is pollinated as quickly as possible
It promotes cross-pollination by preventing self-pollination, increasing genetic variation in offspring
It allows the flower to produce more pollen over time
It prevents insects from visiting the flower too early

questions.explanation: When anthers release pollen before the stigma is receptive (protandry), the flower's own pollen cannot land on its own stigma. This promotes cross-pollination with other plants, increasing genetic variation in the offspring. Greater genetic variation gives the species a better chance of surviving environmental changes.

questions.stem: A plant biologist examines a wind-pollinated grass flower. Which features would she expect to find?

options.text: Large sticky stigmas inside the flower, short stamens, and bright yellow petals
Feathery stigmas hanging outside the flower, long dangling stamens, and small or absent petals
A strong sweet scent, nectaries at the base of petals, and sticky pollen
Thick waxy petals to protect against wind damage

questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers like grasses have feathery stigmas exposed outside the flower to catch airborne pollen, long stamens that dangle in the wind to release pollen easily, and small or absent petals since they do not need to attract insects. Their pollen is light, smooth, and produced in large quantities.

questions.stem: In a flower, the ovary is located at the base of the carpel. After fertilisation, what does the ovary develop into?

options.text: A new flower
A seed
A fruit, which contains the seeds
A pollen grain

questions.explanation: After fertilisation, the ovules inside the ovary develop into seeds, and the ovary wall develops into the fruit. The fruit protects the seeds and aids in their dispersal. This is why fruits are always found surrounding seeds in flowering plants. The ovules become seeds, while the ovary becomes the fruit.
